questions.question: In the EOQ model with planned shortages, with demand rate $D$, setup cost $K$, holding cost $h$ and backlog penalty $p$, which decisions does the policy choose?
options: Only the batch size $y$; the backlog follows from it
The batch size $y$ and the demand rate $D$ per unit time
The stock $s$ and the backlog penalty $p$ per unit time
The batch size $y$ and the stock $s$ after replenishment

questions.question: Compared with the classical EOQ model, which trade-off does the EOQ model with planned shortages (backlog penalty $p$ per unit per unit time) add?
options: Ordering often against holding large batches
Meeting demand against losing customers
Buying cheaply against buying in large lots
Holding stock against making customers wait

questions.question: In the EOQ model with planned shortages, the optimal policy has batch size $y^*$ and stock $s^*$ just after replenishment, with instantaneous replenishment. When is an order placed?
options: When the backlog reaches $y^*-s^*$ units
When the stock on hand has fallen to zero
When the stock on hand falls to $s^*$
When $s^*$ customer units are waiting

questions.question: In the EOQ model with planned shortages (batch size $y$, backlog penalty $p$), what does the decision variable $s$ represent?
options: The maximum number of backlogged customer units
The stock level at which the next order is placed
The stock left after a batch clears the backlog
The average stock held over a whole ordering cycle

questions.question: An EOQ model with planned shortages has setup cost $K=90$ per order, demand $D=100$ units per week, holding cost $h=5$ and backlog penalty $p=4$ per unit per week, so $\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}=60$. Using $y^*=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}\sqrt{\frac{p+h}{p}}$, what is the optimal batch size?
options: 90 units
60 units
40 units
135 units

questions.question: An optimal EOQ policy with planned shortages has holding cost $h=5$ and backlog penalty $p=4$ per unit per week. What fraction of each cycle has stock on hand?

An EOQ model with planned shortages has setup cost $K=90$ per order, demand $D=100$ units per week, holding cost $h=5$ and backlog penalty $p=4$ per unit per week. Using $TCU(y,s)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hs^2}{2y}+\frac{p(y-s)^2}{2y}$, what is the cost rate of the policy $y=90$, $s=40$?
options: 300 per week
144.4 per week
155.6 per week
200 per week

questions.question: In the optimal EOQ policy with planned shortages, the backlog penalty $p$ rises while $h$, $K$ and $D$ stay the same. What happens to the fraction $\frac{p}{p+h}$ of each cycle with stock on hand?
options: It falls, so customers wait for more of each cycle.
It rises, so customers wait for less of each cycle.
It stays the same, as the cycle length does not change.
It jumps to 1 as soon as $p$ exceeds the holding cost $h$.

questions.question: For a finite backlog penalty $p>0$, the optimal batch $y^*=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}\sqrt{\frac{p+h}{p}}$ is larger than $\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}$, the classical batch without shortages. What makes larger batches worthwhile?
options: Backlogged customers order more, so demand per cycle rises.
The backlog penalty $p$ adds to the holding cost $h$.
Part of each batch clears backlog and is never held in stock.
Each setup costs more once shortages are planned in the cycle.

questions.question: In the EOQ model with planned shortages, stock falls from $s$ to 0 and then a backlog builds up until the batch $y$ arrives. Why is the holding cost rate $\frac{hs^2}{2y}$ rather than $\frac{hs}{2}$?
options: Stock averages $\frac{s^2}{2}$ during the whole stock phase.
Holding cost is charged on backlogged units as well as stock.
$\frac{hs}{2}$ is the holding cost of one whole cycle.
Stock is on hand only for a share $\frac{s}{y}$ of each cycle.

questions.question: An optimal EOQ policy with planned shortages has $y^*=90$ units, $s^*=40$ units and demand $D=100$ units per week. For how long are customers waiting in each cycle?
options: 0.4 weeks
0.5 weeks
0.9 weeks
0.25 weeks

questions.question: An EOQ model with planned shortages has $h=5$ and $p=4$ per unit per week, but the batch size is fixed at $y=135$ units by the truck size. Treating $y$ as a constant and setting the derivative of $TCU(y,s)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hs^2}{2y}+\frac{p(y-s)^2}{2y}$ with respect to $s$ to zero, which $s$ is best?

In the EOQ model with planned shortages, what happens to $y^*=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}\sqrt{\frac{p+h}{p}}$ and $s^*=\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}\sqrt{\frac{p}{p+h}}$ as the backlog penalty $p$ grows without bound?
options: $y^*$ grows without bound, while $s^*$ approaches 0 (no stock).
Both approach $\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}$, giving no shortages.
Both approach 0, as any backlog becomes too costly.
$y^*$ approaches $\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}$, while $s^*$ approaches 0.

questions.question: The EOQ model with planned shortages assumes a backlog penalty $p>0$. What would happen to the optimal policy as $p$ approached 0, with $K$, $D$, $h>0$ fixed?
options: It approaches the classical policy without shortages.
$y^*$ and $s^*$ both approach 0: orders become continuous.
$s^*\to0$ while $y^*$ grows without bound: longer cycles.
$s^*\to0$ while $y^*$ stays at $\sqrt{\frac{2KD}{h}}$.

questions.question: For $K=90$, $D=100$ per week, $h=5$ and $p=4$ per unit per week, the optimum $y^*=90$, $s^*=40$ costs 200 per week. A planner uses $y=45$, $s=20$, with the same ratio $\frac{s}{y}=\frac{p}{p+h}=\frac{4}{9}$. Using $TCU(y,s)=\frac{KD}{y}+\frac{hs^2}{2y}+\frac{p(y-s)^2}{2y}$, what is its cost rate?
options: 200 per week, the same as the optimum since the ratio matches
250 per week, so the right ratio alone is not optimal
100 per week, half the cost of the optimal policy
150 per week, as the setup term stays at 100

questions.question: A firm with holding cost $h=5$ per unit per week uses an EOQ policy with planned shortages that is optimal for its backlog penalty $p$, with batch size 90 and stock 40 just after replenishment. Which value of $p$ per unit per week does this policy reveal?
